near_miss.lead: léttr ... fótr ~ ἐλαφρότεροι πόδας ('light of foot')
near_miss.why_not: The cognate pair is exact (léttr = ἐλαφρός, fótr = πούς), but 'light-footed' is a generic idiom. The only Germanic witnesses are two manuscripts of the same St Olaf miracle (DG 8; AM 619 4to 63r), a hagiographic text probably rendering the Latin Passio Olavi, so there is no native Norse continuity. See the search lead for the Homeric divine-healing formula.

search_lead.cognate: ON léttr = Gk ἐλαφρός (*h1lengʷʰ-); fótr = πούς (*pṓd-)
search_lead.argument: In the ON, after the saint's healing the man's foot 'became soft and light' for riding and running. In the Homeric formula γυῖα δ' ἔθηκεν ἐλαφρὰ πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὕπερθεν, a god answering a prayer (Il. 5.122 after Diomedes is wounded) makes the limbs light. Same cognate pair, same divine-restoration context. Weak: generic idiom and a Latin-derived hagiographic witness.

search_lead.cognate: none: ON ósánir (sá < *seh1-) vs Gk ἄσπαρτα (σπείρω); vaxa (*h2weks-) vs φύονται (*bʰuH-). A motif match only.
search_lead.argument: Vǫluspá's renewed world, where 'unsown fields will grow', matches the Homeric paradise-land motif of crops that grow 'unsown and unploughed' (Cyclopes): a negated participle of 'sow' plus 'grow' for land that bears without tillage. Vedic akṛṣṭapacya- 'ripening without ploughing' is the same notion. Every slot is renewed, so it is a typological or golden-age motif and may be Christian-apocalyptic in Vǫluspá. Not claimed. Hesiod WD 117-118 (the earth bears 'of itself' in the golden race) is a further Greek witness to the motif.

near_miss.why_not: Cognate field/sow pair, but it is everyday agricultural wording, the contexts are not congruent (eschatological renewal vs vineyard planting), and the ON point is the negation 'unsown', which Cato lacks; see the search lead for Od. 9.109.

near_miss.lead: hjǫrr til hjarta 'sword to the heart' ~ hṛd ... śalyam
near_miss.why_not: hjǫrr is cognate with Ved. śáru- 'missile', but the Rām. line uses śalya- (not cognate) and is metaphorical grief. No Vedic śáru- + hṛd- collocation found (8 RV śáru hits, none with heart). hjǫrr til hjarta is an alliterative Norse formula (also AM-35-fol 44).

near_miss.lead: 'light' of the eyes (liós ... augu ~ lumina ... oculis)
near_miss.why_not: Light = sight is generic. The ON is a Christian healing-of-the-blind miracle modelled on Latin hagiography (lumen), and Lucretius means death. Not inherited wording.

near_miss.lead: figura etymologica 'bind with bonds' (Bundu ... bandum ~ bandhena baddho / badhyate bandhe)
near_miss.why_not: Cognate verb + instrumental noun of *bʰendʰ-, but any language with both the verb and its derived noun produces this figure freely. Contexts differ (literal iron fetters in a martyrdom vs the 'bond of dharma'). Too generic to claim.
Only tár ~ δάκρυ is cognate. ON 'prayed with tears' is the Latin Christian 'cum lacrimis'; the Homeric 'shed tears' verb (χέω) has no ON counterpart.

near_miss.lead: name of the first (heiti ens fyrsta hofðingia ... nafn ~ prathamásya nā́ma; λαμβάνω ὄνομα)
near_miss.why_not: nafn ~ nā́ma ~ ὄνομα and fyrstr ~ prathamá share roots, but ON is the prose eponym ('the realm takes its name from the first chieftain'), RV is 'knowing the name of the first day', and Hdt is borrowing a god's name. Contexts differ and the verbs (taka / λαμβάνω) are not cognate.

near_miss.lead: fleeing from wolves / hunted with dogs (ar chonaib altaib ~ með hunda)
near_miss.why_not: Both Irish passages are the same Tuan mac Cairill text (one branch). The ON hunting with dogs is a narrative coincidence, not shared wording; Thucydides is irrelevant.

error.correct_reading: hlýtt, past participle of hlýða 'listen' (*ḱlew-): 'er lytt hava' = 'who have listened'
error.evidence: Context 'At þæim læiðizk æigi langmæle vart er lytt hava' (that our long speech not weary those who have listened).

error.correct_reading: vanr 'accustomed, wont' (cf. venja; *wenh1-), not the homograph vanr 'lacking'
error.evidence: 'hunda ... sem þui varo vaner at spyria þa menn upp' = dogs that were used to tracking down men.

error.correct_reading: Hǫðr, the god's name (proper name, should be unmapped like Baldr in the same line)
error.evidence: 'búa þeir Höðr ok Baldr': Höðr paired with Baldr as the two gods.

note: Second reading of 8 flagged bundles: no claims. 8 near-misses, 2 search leads (Homeric divine-healing 'light feet' formula; Vǫluspá unsown fields ~ Od. 9.109/Hes. WD 118 motif), 3 error reports.
